assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki and Moore's credit-cycles model shows how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. It became the template for financial-friction macroeconomics and the analysis of crises, with wide influence on theory and on policy thinking.
assessment.attribution: The core 1997 credit-cycles contribution is clearly jointly Kiyotaki and Moore. Gertler and Gilchrist are important for the financial accelerator and its empirical side, but they form a distinct strand, so I propose the two originators.
assessment.maturity: About three decades of citation, extension and use after the 2008 crisis. Related macro-finance work was recognised in 2022 (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig), but the collateral-constraint mechanism itself has not been.
uncertainties: Overlap with the earlier financial-accelerator recognition of Bernanke could be read as partial coverage.
Whether the committee would prefer to include Gertler for breadth.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection changed international trade. It moved the field from representative-firm models to models of exporter selection, reallocation and a new channel for gains from trade. It also connects to micro data and is widely used in policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) and Helpman's broader synthesis extend it. Redding's contribution is substantial but more recent and more quantitative, so the cleanest credit goes to Melitz and Helpman. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not on this ballot entry and are an attribution risk.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of confirmation in firm-level data and in theoretical and quantitative work. The trade field has had no prize since Krugman in 2008.
uncertainties: Omission of Bernard, Jensen and Eaton-Kortum, who made parallel empirical and theoretical contributions.
Helpman also appears on another ballot entry, which complicates how credit would be divided.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural demand estimation with differentiated products, together with dynamic industry models, underpins modern merger analysis, antitrust and empirical IO. It supplies the practical toolkit for measuring market power and welfare, and it has spread to trade, health and other fields.
assessment.attribution: The BLP demand-estimation framework and Pakes's broader methodological programme (estimation and dynamic games) are the core. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin made important but more distinct or later contributions, so there is some attribution ambiguity at the margin.
assessment.maturity: Three decades of established use in academia, competition authorities and industry. Pakes's work has long been regarded as prize-level.
uncertainties: Whether Bresnahan should displace one of the BLP co-authors.
The seven-name list suggests the credit is diffuse and the three-name cap forces a hard choice.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Their political-economy models of trade protection, especially lobbying in 'Protection for Sale', gave a tractable and empirically testable account of why trade policy departs from free trade. They also shaped the political-economy and empirical trade-policy literatures. The pair's wider endogenous-growth and trade-and-growth work adds to their standing.
assessment.attribution: The credit is clearly joint between Grossman and Helpman, with a small but specific scope. Other contributors to the political economy of trade, such as Mayer and Rodrik, are not on the entry.
assessment.maturity: The foundational papers date from the 1990s and have been tested and extended widely, though empirical support is mixed.
uncertainties: The narrower political-economy contribution may be judged less transformative than the broader Grossman-Helpman agenda.
Ranking this pair alongside a Helpman-Melitz laureate set would raise concerns about crowding out other trade contributors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rubinstein's alternating-offers bargaining model is a cornerstone of non-cooperative game theory. It gave a unique equilibrium and a standard foundation for modelling negotiation, and it is used across labour, industrial organisation and political economy. Rubinstein-Wolinsky extended it to decentralised markets.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein is the central figure. Wolinsky's contribution on bargaining in markets is distinct and significant. Binmore's contributions are important for interpretation, refinement and experimental links but more secondary.
assessment.maturity: Over forty years of confirmation as a canonical model. Game theory has been recognised repeatedly, so a later award in this area competes with other fields.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would favour Rubinstein alone.
Prior game-theory prizes may reduce the priority of this area.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities, together with the theory of optimal monetary policy built on it, is the dominant paradigm in central-bank policy analysis. Its practical influence is very large.
assessment.attribution: Credit is highly diffuse across eight names. Calvo (pricing), Taylor (rules), Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans and Smets-Wouters (estimated DSGE), Clarida-Gali-Gertler and Woodford (the core synthesis) all contributed. Any three-name selection necessarily omits major figures.
assessment.maturity: Established over about 25 years, but the framework was challenged after 2008 and during the recent inflation episode, and its scope is still being revised.
uncertainties: Severe attribution ambiguity, with Taylor, Calvo and Clarida among the omitted names.
Debates about the framework's performance after 2008 and in the recent inflation surge.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Their political-economics work on electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity brought formal modelling and empirical identification to the study of how political institutions shape fiscal and economic outcomes. It is a coherent research programme with wide reach.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the closest pair through their joint book and papers. Besley's work on state capacity and accountability is closely related but separate. The credit is relatively clear within the trio.
assessment.maturity: More than three decades of development and confirmation. The 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity recognised an adjacent area, which may lower urgency.
uncertainties: Possible perceived overlap with the 2024 recognition of institutions and growth.
Heterogeneity within the programme makes the exact prize motivation harder to specify.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work on import competition from China and on technology and tasks changed how economists and policymakers think about labour-market adjustment, wage inequality and trade's distributional effects. It is highly influential in policy debate and brings credible empirical designs to a central question.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock papers are clearly Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The tasks and technology strand has Autor as the key figure, with Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane as important contributors who are not on this entry. Katz's role is mainly in the earlier skill-biased-change literature.
assessment.maturity: The China-shock results are about a decade old. They have been confirmed in several settings, but some findings on magnitudes and mechanisms are still debated, so maturity is lower than for the older candidates above.
uncertainties: Ongoing debate about the magnitude and persistence of the trade-shock effects.
Overlap with the 2024 and 2025 prizes' themes on technology and growth, and with Acemoglu's tasks work, which complicates attribution.
